prayer.text: Saint Gertrude the Great, pray for us.

cues.text: A Child Given to God
Gertrude was born on January 6, 1256, the feast of the Epiphany.
Nothing is known of her parents or of her birthplace.
At about the age of five, in 1261, she entered the monastery of Helfta in Saxony to be educated.
She would spend her whole life within its walls.
Helfta was then governed by the Abbess Gertrude of Hackeborn, under whom the house prospered in monastic observance and in learning.
The child was placed in the care of Mechtilde, the abbess's sister and the mistress of the school.
The Catholic Encyclopedia warns that the abbess must not be confused with Gertrude the Great.
The abbess wrote nothing and has not been canonized.
A Gifted and Restless Student
Gertrude proved an exceptional student.
She mastered the trivium and the quadrivium, the course of study of her age.
She loved literature, music, song and the painting of miniatures.
In later years she described her youth as a time of spiritual blindness.
Benedict XVI portrays a young woman of strong, determined and impulsive temperament.
The Catholic Encyclopedia finds in her no sudden leap from sin to holiness.
Her struggle, it says, lay in mastering a sensitive and impetuous nature.
The Wounds of the Lord
In Advent of 1280, Gertrude grew weary of her studies and saw how empty they were.
Then, on January 27, 1281, near the hour of Compline, an inner light eased her anguish.
In her own account, a young man took her by the hand and showed her his wounds.
She recognized them as the wounds of Jesus, who saved us by his Blood on the Cross.
This is a private revelation, reported in her own writings.
The Church does not require anyone to believe it.
From that day her friendship with the Lord deepened.
The Catholic Encyclopedia places her first vision in her twenty-sixth year.
After it, she turned from secular studies to Scripture, the Fathers and theology.
In its words, she "from being a grammarian became a theologian.
A Pen in the Service of the Church
Gertrude read, copied, translated and wrote for the spiritual good of others.
She cited Augustine and Jerome, and very often St. Bernard of Clairvaux .
Her best known work is the Herald of Divine Love , in Latin the Legatus Divinae Pietatis .
It has five books.
Only the second is Gertrude's own.
The others were compiled by members of the Helfta community, who recorded the favors God granted her.
She also left the Spiritual Exercises , seven meditations running from the grace of baptism to preparation for death.
Theologians of the Dominican and Franciscan orders examined her writings and approved them.
Much of what she wrote was lost when Helfta was destroyed.
The Heart of Christ
Gertrude's spirituality is rooted in the Rule of St. Benedict and in the liturgy.
Her prayer was shaped by Advent and Christmas, by Lent and Easter, and by the feasts of Our Lady.
The Catholic Encyclopedia calls devotion to the Sacred Heart the mark of her piety.
Benedict XVI notes that she wrote of being admitted into the intimacy of the Divine Heart of Christ.
We can hear this nearness in the prayer of her Seventh Exercise, written to prepare for death.
From her life Benedict XVI drew a lesson for every age.
A happy and true life rests on friendship with the Lord Jesus.
A Hidden Life of Charity
Outwardly, Gertrude lived as a simple Benedictine nun.
Her charity, the Catholic Encyclopedia says, embraced rich and poor, learned and simple.
She felt tender sympathy for the souls in purgatory.
Her humility was so deep that she asked that outward signs of her spiritual gifts be avoided.
She outlived her teacher Mechtilde, who died in 1298, and the Abbess Gertrude, who died in 1291.
Gertrude died at Helfta, near Eisleben, on November 17, in 1301 or 1302.
She was in her forty-fifth or forty-sixth year.
The place of her burial is unknown, and no record of any translation of her body survives.
Legacy
In 1677 her name was inscribed in the Roman Martyrology, and her feast was extended to the universal Church.
Today the Church keeps her memory on November 16 as an optional memorial.
At the request of the King of Spain, she was declared patroness of the West Indies.
St. Teresa of Ávila chose her as a model and guide.
St. Francis de Sales also numbered among her admirers.
Benedict XVI observed that she is the only German woman to bear the title of Great, a title won by her cultural and spiritual influence.
After more than four centuries, Helfta was restored in 1999, and nuns live there once again.
She remains for us a teacher of friendship with Christ, hidden in a cloister yet near to every heart.
